claims.text: Single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys can retain high yield strength and resist softening at elevated temperatures.
NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 exhibits a high-temperature yield-strength plateau.
NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 has stable elastic moduli at elevated temperatures.
Edge dislocations can dominate plastic deformation in BCC refractory high-entropy alloys rather than the screw dislocations typical of conventional BCC metals.
Edge-dislocation-dominant deformation governs the high-temperature strength and thermoelastic behavior of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5.
Chemical complexity produces lattice distortions that enhance the edge-dislocation mechanism.
Homogenization at approximately 1400 °C for 24 hours eliminates microsegregation while retaining a single-phase alloy.
An additional anneal near 850 °C can enhance short-range order while maintaining the single-phase BCC structure.
The SRO-promoting anneal creates stronger lattice-distortion features than are present in the homogenized baseline.
Short-range order and its associated lattice distortions increase the Peierls barrier for edge-dislocation motion.
Lattice distortion in the chemically complex alloy hampers conventional screw-dislocation motion.
SRO makes local distortion fields more pronounced and thereby increases the barrier to edge-dislocation glide.
Edge dislocations are less sensitive than screw dislocations to thermally activated double-kink nucleation.
Reduced thermal sensitivity of edge-dislocation motion causes the high-temperature yield-strength plateau.
The proposed edge-dislocation mechanism also causes stable thermoelastic moduli at elevated temperatures.
Relative to the homogenized baseline, the SRO-enhanced alloy will have a higher or more temperature-stable yield-strength plateau.
Relative to the baseline, the SRO-enhanced alloy will have a slightly higher or more temperature-stable elastic modulus.
The SRO-enhanced sample will show a greater prevalence of impeded edge dislocations than the baseline.

The comparison is intended to apply only while the alloy remains single-phase BCC without precipitation or phase separation, at temperatures up to about 1073 K under controlled strain rate and inert atmosphere.

Failure to observe statistically significant strength retention or appreciably different modulus behavior, together with no evidence of enhanced edge-dislocation impediment, would falsify the proposed SRO-based explanation.
